title: How Crying Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant open with an announcement about a live SXSW podcast (March 11, Maximilian Room, Driscoll Hotel) and a free public Variety Show viewing party for a Science Channel TV pilot (March 12, Fado Irish Pub, Austin), then discuss how crying works: the three types of tears (basal, reflex, emotional), the composition of onion versus sad-movie tears, whether crying makes people feel better and cultural views on it (Japanese crying clubs), infant crying and its possible evolutionary origins, manipulative crying, gender differences and prolactin, the Rosey Grier "Greer effect" on men crying, health links to stress and depression, and tears' social bonding role. The episode closes with a listener mail from Lori in Germany about a Muppet Christmas Carol scare and a how stuff works Muppets article, plus site and contact information.

entities.name: Free to Be... You and Me

segments.title: Opening banter and event announcements
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about Rosey Grier's 'Free to Be... You and Me' song, then announce a live SXSW podcast on March 11 and a free public Variety Show viewing party for the Science Channel TV pilot on March 12 at Fado Irish Pub in Austin.
topics: Free to Be... You and Me

segments.title: Can animals cry and the Cocoa gorilla video
segments.summary: Hosts discuss whether elephants and gorillas cry emotionally, mention the Water for Elephants premiere story, and describe the Cocoa gorilla video where she reacts to her kitten's death.

segments.title: Types of tears and basal tear production
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the three types of tears: basal, reflex, and emotional. They note that people produce about five to ten ounces of basal tears daily, which drain through the sinuses, and define tears as secretions of fats, proteins, mucus, oil, and mostly water.

segments.title: Why onions make you cry
segments.summary: The hosts explain reflex tears using onions: cutting an onion releases lachrymatory factor synthase, which leads to a compound that irritates the lacrimal glands. Chuck talks about wearing goggles.

segments.title: Emotional tear chemistry and whether crying helps
segments.summary: The hosts describe the theory that emotional tears are triggered by the cerebrum and endocrine system. A study compared onion tears with sad-movie tears, finding sad tears contain prolactin, ACTH, and leucine enkephalin. Research on whether crying improves mood is mixed, with one study showing two low-mood days before and after crying.

segments.title: Cultural views on crying and crying clubs
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why studies on crying's benefits may be unrealistic in labs, including the helplessness factor and lack of consolation. They describe Japanese crying clubs and the idea that the cultural belief that crying helps affects whether people report feeling better.

segments.title: Infant crying and its evolutionary origins
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why babies cry and a hypothesis from a study that crying evolved through natural selection, since crying reduces infanticide and signals a healthy baby. They also cover how babies' cries change with age and manipulative crying around ten months.

segments.title: Gender differences, prolactin, and the men-crying debate
segments.summary: The hosts describe how crying changes at adolescence with testosterone and estrogen, cite William Frey's prolactin claim, and mention a study that counted yearly crying (about 64 times for women versus 17 for men). They then discuss the claim that men cry less because of smaller tear ducts and the Greer effect, plus examples of public male crying such as Tim Tebow.

segments.title: Health, depression, and social bonding of tears
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the idea that stress hormones leave the body through tears and that holding in emotions may be bad for health. They cover a study on crying and mood disorders, postpartum depression, PTSD, and an Israeli study where tear smell reduced sexual arousal, supporting a social bonding theory.

segments.title: Listener mail from Lori in Germany
segments.summary: Lori, an English teacher at a German kindergarten, writes that after showing A Muppet Christmas Carol, a six-year-old was frightened by the ghosts. She showed the kids the Muppets article on HowStuffWorks, which helped calm the child.

segments.title: Outro and how crying works article
segments.summary: The hosts point listeners to the How Crying Works article on TLC.com and invite listener contact through Twitter, Facebook, and email. They also promote the Stuff from the Future video podcast.
